I think we should focus less on the fact that is was not the Google car's fault. I get it, the other guy rear ended it, and the self-driving car is probably safer than a human driver on average. However, we should still acknowledge that accidents WILL happen; they are bound to happen, if you have the smallest faith in statistics. And at some point, one of those cars IS going to make something stupid. All we have to do is ensure proper policies are in place to account for that, we don't have to believe that nothing bad will ever happen in order to defend the initiative.

I do think every self-driving car should have a fall-back manual system in place, though. If the unpredictable happens, being able to take control might just well save a life.

How would your proposed manual mode work? Or better, what would that do to save lives? The driver would first have to recognize a potential danger, then switch to manual mode (possibly in a panic), and then finally begin to take control of the vehicle. All of these steps take time, an amount that may seem insignificant at first glance but quickly becomes a serious issue as the speed of thw vehicle increases.

I'm not saying you're wrong in desiring a manual override, but there would be some serious hurdles to overcome before a system like that could be considered a safety improvement.
A better idea is to just have the car pull over as soon as it's safe. There should be a critical emergency mode, stored on a second computer, just in case something is wrong on the main.

On the spot, I can imagine one simple situation: car gets stranded in snow in a bad winter day, some sensors fail or whatever and it won't move at all. A reasonably experienced driver, if only allowed to, can take control and leave a situation that could be fatal in a matter of hours.
